title: Henningsvaer Pride
description: I built a concept website for Henningsvær’s Pride celebrations using Next.js, Tailwind, GSAP, Sanity, and some WebGL magic.

The main idea was to explore how Next.js and Sanity work together. It turned out to be a really intuitive setup — both for developers and clients — since Sanity essentially lets you design your own CMS.

At the same time, I was experimenting with WebGL shaders. The site’s background uses a custom gradient shader I made by hand, which I later optimized for performance with React Three Fiber. Originally, the homepage had a GIF for the Pride flag, but once I realized how simple it was to build my own animated shader flag, I switched it out.
Working with GSAP was another highlight. It integrated smoothly with Next.js, and even small animations made the site feel much more alive.
Some of the projects features include:
• Fetching & visualising content from Sanity
• A custom Sanity Studio setup for editing
• Locale-based content (/en & /no) with translations pulled from a custom JSON dictionary
• GSAP & WebGL animations
• A fully custom design built from scratch
Overall, I had a great time designing the site, building the UI/UX, and structuring the CMS. It was a solid learning experience and left me excited to create more projects with this kind of stack!

title: Custom Shopify setup
description: Around mid-2024, during my travels, I decided to start exploring how to build custom e-commerce sites — specifically by setting up my own NUXT 3 + Shopify integration.

Most Shopify templates you can buy or use for free tend to feel a bit dull. I get why they’re great for startups or small businesses who want to launch fast, but to me, they often feel like a “one-size-fits-all” solution. I wanted to see how much effort it would take to create something simple, customisable, and a bit more fun — something that could potentially be a solid alternative for these businesses.

I hadn’t worked much with GraphQL before, so learning how to structure the data and write the queries took some getting used to. But once I got the hang of it, the development process felt smooth and straightforward.

I chose to work with NUXT 3 because Vue has been my favourite framework so far. I’d briefly used NUXT before during my Gazelle project and found it intuitive and flexible. Pairing it with Pinia gave me a lot of control over state management, allowing me to build something with great performance.

There’s still a bunch of improvements and updates I want to add over time — and I will — but as a baseline for smaller Shopify projects, I’m pretty happy with where it’s at. Shaping it to fit a client’s needs should be smooth sailing from here B).
What inspired me?
• I took a lot of inspiration from sites like:
• Fawbooks
• Blue Marble Paris
• Voostore
• Tur Snowboards
• Pleasures
• Braindead
I spent quite a bit of time digging into the small details that make modern e-com sites feel good — finding those little silver linings that make the user experience smooth, fun, and effective.
Wanna try it out?
If you’re curious and want to check out the setup — or even use it yourself — you can find the project here: github.com/Muridae-dev/shopify-nuxt-integration.
Feel free to drop a PR if you’ve got ideas or improvements — or just reach out to me via email if you have any questions!

title: Gazelle
description: This was my second proper project at DEPT — working all the way from scratch to release — and it was my first time working with NUXT in a professional setting.

It was just me and a colleague of mine as frontend devs, which I really enjoyed. We hit it off from the start & work-wise, we made project decisions fast and effective and had lots of great discussions around different coding solutions. Together we built a great relationship with the client, which made the whole process smooth and fun.

Some things could’ve been more effective — we were lacking some structure at times, mostly due to the absence of a project manager — but with time, we worked out those kinks, and the two of us really stepped up during the process.
What were some of my proudest moments?
• Worked extensively with the client’s API — which data-wise was a mess — structuring the data and saving bits to our store to reduce redundant calls.
• Used the data to create multiple dynamic solutions, such as the color and model picker for each individual bike model.

• Managed to integrate our client’s API with Google Maps, even though I hadn’t worked with map-based solutions before. The problem-solving involved here gave me a serious challenge, and I was thrilled to get it working.
• Building and fostering a great relationship within the team and with the client.
• All the discussions and solutions I worked on with my colleague. It taught me a lot about Vue, NUXT, and coding in general.
Technologies used within the project consisted mainly of:
• NUXT.js
• Pinia
• Storyblok
• Client's APIs

title: Ramboll.com
description: This was my first project at DEPT, starting off as a trainee. I asked around wherever I could for projects — as at the time frontend work was somewhat scarce — and I managed to get a position on this project from the start.

Me and the team worked together from a POC all the way to a final release, and it taught me a lot. Getting to work with NEXT.js, working & communicating with clients, doing presentations, discussions with the team, deadlines — all that good stuff.

I applied myself to take a strong role within the team, putting myself out there whenever I could & it paid off. I got a lot of responsibilities, like handling communications with the client, making project decisions, calculating risk, structuring the project, and so on.
What were some of my proudest moments?

• I did the entire header structure and logic for the website. Although looking back I could’ve done a better job at structuring it — some of the logic behind multiple sections could’ve been more slick, especially on mobile — I managed to get it to a good working state, where the client had multiple choices between header sections and selections.
• Worked on a search/filtering system within their open positions page and their contact us page, grabbing data from their API and posting only the necessary data for each individual search.
• Holding sprint presentations for the client.
• Building & fostering a great relationship within the team and with the client.
Technologies used within the project consisted mainly of:
• NEXT.js
• Kontent.AI
• Client's API

title: SavemissX
description: Being a fan of video-games throughout my life, I’ve wanted to try my hand at making one myself & although this wasn’t my first game, it was the first one I was truly proud of. Having created a game in Java before, I found the language Haxeflixel & I started off following a tutorial to get a gist of how the language worked.

Once I had the tutorial down, I started tinkering with the code & turned the top-down dungeon crawler to a fast paced 2d side-scroller with elements of Super Smash Bros. I used a tool called Aseprite to create the visuals and animations & OGMO Editor to create the maps.

I created: 7 different stages with 3 different backgrounds, character features such as: double jumping, climbing, running, 5 unique attacks & animations and a power up feature called RAGE. The game also features 2 kinds of enemies, a flying- and a grounded enemy.

Working with the game turned into a game itself, gaining new code-knowledge allowed me to “unlock” new features for the game & kept inspiring me to find clever- out of the box solutions to keep updating the game. I really had a blast working on this & I’m stoked to keep exploring new possibilities of game-development / gamification!

title: DODGETHEVIRUS
description: This is DODGE THE VIRUS! It’s an escape-room type game where you have to navigate through funky websites in order to reach THE DRAGON & solve his riddles. During your journey, you’ll have to avoid malicious websites that give you a VIRUS. Being a victim of a VIRUS breaks the game & you’ll need to restart in order to continue.

This was my first task at Hyper Island where we were introduced to HTML, CSS & Javascript. Our task was to simply create a website that utilised each language in some way. I wanted to try out as many features as I could so I decided to make a whole bunch of websites to try different features & strung them all together.

All the pages are native HTML/CSS/JS with a touch of jQuery & everything is loaded dynamically through objects. It ended up turning into kind of a low-end “component-based framework” which at the time I had no idea what it was, so it was a happy surprise to see later on in my studies that web-development is heading in that direction!

title: Marketplace
description: During my studies at Hyper Island we had a Data-interaction module & our task was to request or post information from/to a server. I wanted to try out both methods so I decided to create a Marketplace, somewhat similar to E-bay where users can create accounts, post items to the market & trade items with other users.
I built a MERN-stack working together with a Mongodb server, used bcrypt for user-registration & login, user authentication through JSON-webtokens & saving images to the server using Multer.

In the marketplace you can view other users' item, filter said items using tags & REQUEST TRADEs. The owner of a trade-requested item will be notified in the Inventory and can then choose to ACCEPT TRADE, which will lead to the requesting user to receive said item in their inventory.

title: The Hills
description: During my Hyper Island studies, we tackled 'The Hills,' a collaborative project emphasizing Agile methodologies and MERN-stack development. My prior experience led me to propose and spearhead the MERN-stack setup, guiding our diverse team through its implementation. Engaging in pair- and mob-programming, we embraced weekly sprints, daily standups, and role rotations between scrum master and project owner, enriching our understanding through diverse perspectives.

The project challenge was to conceptualize a product beyond our deadline's scope, focusing on customer value. We envisioned a virtual real estate app allowing users to buy, customize apartments with in-app currency, and explore progressively upscale options. Although we couldn't complete the app, our interactive demo, powered by a Mongodb-database, showcased editable apartments, effectively conveying our vision and demonstrating potential value to users.

title: Blackjack
description: This project was when I was introduced to component based frameworks. Our brief was to use React and build an app together with an API. Most open-source APIs I found were uninspiring, but I found one that stuck out, which was the deck of cards API.

I chose to use the API to simulate BLACKJACK, simple I thought at first, however, it was a bit more complicated than I anticipated. Due to the rules of the game, there’s quite a lot to consider: first off there’s betting, you can ask for more cards, you can bust -losing due to too high value-, Aces automatically going between 11 and 1, and creating a system for the dealer AI.
I had a lot of fun with the challenge & it was surprisingly fitting to use a component based framework for Blackjack, using cards, hands, players, and pot as separate components.

title: Tombraiders
description: This was my third group project at Hyper Island where our brief was to create a game within Phaser, a framework used to make games in Javascript.

I was chosen to lead the team throughout the process, my tasks were structuring weekly sprints & tickets for the team to cover, holding workshops to explain the basics of game-design & making sure the team's ideas would come through in a time-efficient manner.

We ended up creating a 2d-platformer called “Tombraiders”, we used Phaser for the in-game features and a tile map editor called Tiled for the maps. The game includes features such as double-jumping, attacking, enemy AI, keys to unlock doors, and 4 different levels.

title: Honorable Mentions
description: These are some of the minor projects & accomplishments I’ve worked on throughout the years:

In 2024, right before leaving DEPT, I created a tracking script for the website Soho Home, hooked up to software within Salesforce Commerce Cloud to track user behavior on the website using third-party cookies. Tracking would consist of:

• Stitching together a profile for each user navigating the website; this would start with grabbing their IP and adding data such as email, name, etc., whenever they would provide that information anywhere on the website.
• Tracking which types of pages the user navigated to.
• What items they added to their carts, including data such as categories, collections, quantities, price-tags, etc.
• Checkout process & how far they got in said process.
• Creating a “schema” of what types of sub-pages users would navigate to, e.g., collection-, product-, home-page, etc.

It was a pretty tough challenge since the integration was run in third-party software. While lots of the code was written in native JavaScript, there were many third-party scripts I had to learn on short notice with somewhat lackluster documentation. That being said, I had a lot of fun on the project as it involved a lot of problem-solving and outside-the-box thinking.

I was really happy with the end result; the script ended up being streamlined, well-structured for future developers to pick up, and worked surprisingly well — especially considering the initial circumstances. Both I, the client, and DEPT were really happy with my efforts!
<hr>

After leaving DEPT, I started picking up some side projects while I was figuring out my life back in Stockholm. One of them was to create a custom E-commerce solution for Shopify. I know some people who have created their own Shopify shops using the built-in templates, and while it does a good job of getting your shop live on short notice, I feel like it lacks personal charm and performance.

So, I made my own Shopify account and started playing around with their API. I’m a big fan of VUE/NUXT, so I decided to hook the API up with NUXT. Initially, it was pretty overwhelming; I had a hard time finding concrete examples of NUXT + Shopify, and having never touched GraphQL before, I got stuck before even getting started.
However, with some patience, stitching together solutions from different corners of the internet, and some back-and-forth discussions with ChatGPT, I got a working POC up and running. It included:
• Displaying products from my Shopify store on different parts of the site.
• Having products categorized by collections.
• Saving products to a cart.
• Providing a custom checkout link to said cart.

The plan was to learn how to develop E-commerce sites from scratch using NUXT and create a baseline if I’m ever to pick up any custom Shopify projects in the future, and in that, I feel like I succeeded.
You can find the project on my GitHub.
<hr>

I worked for TeamTownSports, an E-commerce site for a Canadian sporting retailer, at the end of my tenure at DEPT. By the time I got into the project, they had just gone live, meaning lots of team members were starting to drop off. The plan was for me to take over all the front-end responsibilities over the course of a month or two.

It was set up with Salesforce Commerce Cloud (SFCC) and was hooked up to DEPT’s own TamTam setup. It wasn’t my cup of tea in terms of framework, and my tasks consisted mostly of bug-fixing. However, the team was really fun to work with, and since I was the sole front-end developer, I got lots of responsibilities in terms of:
• Presentations
• Communications with the client
• Creating and structuring tickets
• Setting realistic expectations
<hr>

At the start of my tenure at DEPT, I was put on the “service desk” — DEPT’s department for long-term site maintenance. What that meant was that I was given tickets on finished projects that had minor bugs, issues, and/or wanted to add new smaller features.

It was a good learning experience, as I had to locate, download, and orient myself in multiple projects and then find the issues that needed looking into. I got pretty good at “code investigation,” finding ways to locate bugs in live environments, locally, and in the code, then solving them.
